claim: 1. Bread price in Berlin over time (official series)
figures: Statistisches Reichsamt table 'Brotpreis in Berlin', price of 1 kg rye bread (with wheat flour added), monthly. January values as read from the OCR: 1913 29 Pf; 1914 27; 1915 37; 1916 40; 1917 34; 1918 45 Pf; 1919 53 Pf; 1920 118 Pf; 1921 237 Pf; 1922 390 Pf; 1923 250 (marks). 1923 column as read: Jan 250; Feb 389; Mar 463.6; Apr 474; May 482.5; Jun 1,428; Jul 3,466; Aug 69 (thousand); Sep '1612' (thousand; Bundestag gives 1.5 million, so probably 1,512); Oct '1743' (million; Bundestag gives 174 million, so probably 174.3); Nov 201 (billion); Dec 399 (billion). A separate weekly table (Stichtage) as read: 5 Nov 78; 12 Nov 64; 19 Nov 233; 26 Nov 428; 3 Dec 467; 10 Dec 400; 17 Dec 378; 24 Dec 356; 31 Dec 356 (billion marks; the reader could not confirm which of two columns is bread).
fragments: Preis für 1 kg Roggenbrot (mit Zusatz von Weizenmehl)
3. Dezember 467 1200
source_name: Statistisches Reichsamt, Zahlen zur Geldentwertung in Deutschland 1914 bis 1923 (Sonderheft 1 zu Wirtschaft und Statistik), Berlin: Reimar Hobbing 1925, tables on pp. 34-35
read_how: page text (OCR of a scanned table, garbled; units and columns partly inferred)
note: This is the primary source behind the circulating figures. It explains them: 250 = January 1923 monthly average; 201 billion = November 1923 monthly average; 399 billion = December 1923 monthly average; 233 billion = 19 November; 428 billion = 26 November (weekly reference day). The 1923 values from August on and the weekly column assignment are OCR readings and must be checked against the scan before a figure is shown on screen. The values agree with the Bundestag series and with the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns (233 billion on 19 Nov).

claim: 1. Bread price series 1919-1923
figures: Bread (unit and place NOT stated on the page): Dec 1919 0.80 M; Jan 1923 250 M; Aug 1923 69,000 M; Sep 1.5 million; Oct 174 million; Nov 1923 201 billion.
fragments: So stieg der nominelle Brotpreis, der im Dezember 1919 noch bei 0,80 Mark gelegen hatte, im Laufe des Jahres 1923 in astronomische Höhen:
Lag er im Januar 1923 bereits bei 250 Mark, stieg er im August auf 69.000 Mark,
im September auf 1,5 Millionen Mark, im Oktober auf 174 Millionen Mark

claim: 1. Bread price, Berlin, dated days in 1923
figures: 1 kg rye bread in Berlin: 163 marks on 3 Jan 1923; 233 billion marks on 19 Nov 1923. 1 kg beef: 1,800 marks on 3 Jan 1923; 4 trillion 800 billion marks on 19 Nov 1923.

the corresponding prices were 233 billion marks and 4 trillion 800 billion marks on 19 November 1923.

claim: 1. Bread price, eyewitnesses in Berlin, October-November 1923
figures: Betty Scholem, Berlin: 15 Oct 1923 a standard loaf 540 million 'today'; 23 Oct 1923 bread 900 million, 2.5 billion, 5.5 billion in three days (dollar 10, 18.5, 40 billion). Käthe Kollwitz, end of Nov 1923: a loaf 140 billion, then put back down to 80 billion.

Der Dollar sprang in 3 Tagen so: 10 Milliarden, 18½, 40 Milliarden.

Ein Brot 140 Milliarden!
Dann wieder runtergesetzt auf 80 Milliarden.
source_name: GHDI (German Historical Institute Washington): Betty Scholem, letters of 15 and 23 Oct 1923 (Mutter und Sohn im Briefwechsel, C.H. Beck 1989, pp. 84-89); Käthe Kollwitz, Die Tagebücher (1989), pp. 543-44, 561-63
note: The first three fragments are Scholem, the last two Kollwitz. Kollwitz's 'runtergesetzt' fits the official weekly table, which also falls between 5 and 12 November.

figures: Commemorative medal (Domäne Dahlem): 1 pound of bread 3 billion on 1 Nov 1923, 260 billion on 1 Dec 1923. De Nederlandsche Bank: a pound of bread 260 billion on 1 Dec 1923. Berliner Zeitung: a roll (Schrippe) 1 million on 1 Oct, 3 billion on 6 Nov; a kilo of rye bread 5.5 billion at the start of the week and 78 billion at its end. Smithsonian: a pound of rye bread more than 100 billion by November 1923.
fragments: So kostete z.B. 1 Pfd. Brot am 1.11. 3 Milliarden und einen Monat später 260 Milliarden Mark.
a pound of bread cost a whopping 260 billion marks on 1 December 1923.
eine Schrippe kostet am 1. Oktober eine Million Mark, am 6. November drei Milliarden Mark.
am Anfang der Woche kostet ein Kilo Roggenbrot 5,5 Milliarden, am Ende 78 Milliarden.
A pound of rye bread cost more than 100 billion marks by November 1923.

note: Pound versus kilo explains part of the spread. The Berliner Zeitung sentence does not name the week in the fragment I was given (the reader placed it at the end of October / start of November 1923): check before using. 5.5 billion matches Betty Scholem's 23 October figure.

read_how: page text (OCR table; rows 1 Aug-31 Dec 1923 re-read raw)
note: 100 billion marks from 1 December 1923 is confirmed (i.e. AFTER stabilisation, as the paper-mark price of 10 pfennig). The table as read has a single row 12-30 November at 10 billion, with a footnote marker; a local-press article (Schwäbische, 11 Jan 2024) mentions a letter that cost 20 billion, undated, so there may have been steps inside those weeks that the table does not show. Do not say '10 billion until the end of November' without a second source. A stamp-collectors' page confirms the 10-19 Oct 1923 period at 5 million. Betty Scholem's letter of 15 Oct 1923 cost 15 million (probably the foreign rate; she was writing to her son abroad).

claim: 2. One egg, a litre of milk, a kilo of potatoes in Berlin, 9 June and 2 December 1923
figures: Berlin, 9 June 1923: 1 egg 800 M; 1 litre milk 1,440 M; 1 kg potatoes 5,000 M; tram ride 600 M; dollar 100,000 M. Berlin, 2 Dec 1923: 1 egg 320 billion; 1 litre milk 360 billion; 1 kg potatoes 90 billion; tram ride 50 billion; dollar 4.21 trillion.
fragments: For example, on June 9, 1923, an egg in Berlin cost 800 marks; on December 2, it already cost 320 billion marks.
Am 9. Juni 1923 kostete in Berlin:
1 Liter Milch – 1440 Mark
Am 2. Dezember 1923 kostete in Berlin:
1 Ei – 320 Milliarden Mark
Ein Ei kostete 320 Milliarden Mark, ein Kilo Kartoffeln 90 Milliarden und eine Straßenbahnfahrt 50 Milliarden.
source_name: Prof. Hans Frambach (Univ. Wuppertal) interview, 30 Sep 2021; Planet Wissen (WDR), Gregor Delvaux de Fenffe; Armin Fuhrer, Berliner Zeitung 4 Jun 2022
note: None of these pages names the original source of the list. The two tram figures in it disagree with the Statistisches Reichsamt table (see tram entry), so treat the whole list as secondary. 2 December 1923 is after the mark was stabilised (20 November): these are the last paper-mark prices, not prices 'at the height of the inflation'.

claim: 2. Butter, rice, milk, eggs, meat, shoes: other dated prices
figures: Butter: a kilo 3,600 M early Jan 1923, 18,000 early April, 72,000 early July (Berliner Zeitung). Kroner, Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung 26 Aug 1923: rice 80,000 marks a pound yesterday, 160,000 today; butter 'instead of 1,600,000 marks, just 1,400,000' (unit not stated). Letter from Berlin 2 Feb 1923: a litre of milk 560 marks. Letter 17 Feb 1923 (dollar at 19,000): meat 15-18 cents a pound; butter etc. 30-35 cents a pound; 1 egg 2 cents; 1 loaf of bread 20 cents; coal 45 cents a hundredweight. Mittagszeitung 17 Feb 1923: shoes 60,000 to 120,000 marks (3.5 to 6.5 dollars); an iron 2-litre cooking pot 30,000 marks.
fragments: Ein Kilo Butter kostet Anfang Januar 3600 Mark, Anfang April 18.000 Mark und Anfang Juli 72.000 Mark
Rice, 80,000 marks a pound yesterday, costs 160,000 marks today
Cheaper butter! Instead of 1,600,000 marks, just 1,400,000 marks.
A liter of milk now costs 560 marks.
1 egg = 2 cents !!!
Here, shoes still cost between 60,000 and 120,000 marks or 3½ to 6½ dollars
source_name: Michael Brettin, Berliner Zeitung 15 Nov 2017; Friedrich Kroner, 'Überreizte Nerven', Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung 26 Aug 1923 (trans. Weimar Republic Sourcebook, 1994, pp. 63-64) via GHDI doc. 3841; GHDI doc. 5414, letters of 'Wolfgang' to Edgar Stillman Kelley, 2 and 17 Feb 1923, with a Mittagszeitung clipping of 17 Feb 1923
note: Kroner and the February letters are primary sources. The Berliner Zeitung butter figures are unsourced on the page.

claim: 2. A glass of beer; a newspaper; a cup of coffee
figures: Beer: Smithsonian gives a glass of beer 150 million marks and a pound of potatoes 50 million, with no date in the sentence (context autumn 1923). Earlier: Hemingway at Kehl, Sept 1922, beer 10 marks a stein; Goodman: in 1922 milk went from 7 to 16 marks a litre and beer from 5.6 to 18. Coffee: Victor Klemperer's diary, early August 1923: board showed 6,000 M, waiter asked 12,000. Newspaper: NO dated price found.
fragments: A pound of potatoes and a glass of beer, staples of the German diet,
came in at 50 million and 150 million marks, respectively.
Beer was 10 marks a stein, or 1-1/4 cents.
Milk went from 7 Marks per liter to 16; beer from 5.6 to 18.
source_name: Smithsonian Magazine, 'How Hyperinflation Heralded the Fall of German Democracy'; Ernest Hemingway, Toronto Daily Star 19 Sep 1922 (GHDI); George J.W. Goodman ('Adam Smith'), Paper Money (1981), pp. 57-62, on PBS Commanding Heights
note: The Smithsonian beer/potato figures cannot be dated from the page: do not attach a month. 'A wheelbarrow full of money would not even buy a newspaper' (Goodman; repeated by Britannica) is a figure of speech with no price or source behind it. A 2023 working paper (Brunnermeier et al.) says newspaper prices 'were also adjusted at shorter and shorter intervals' but gives no figure in the part read.

claim: 3. Wages paid daily; paid in the lunch break; money fetched in handcarts and sacks
figures: Weekly pay became daily pay, then payment in the lunch break; workers fetched pay with handcarts (Leiterwagen), notes paid out by the sack.
fragments: Firmen gingen von wöchentlicher zu täglicher Lohnzahlung über und weiter zur Zahlung in der Mittagspause.
Ihren Lohn holten die Arbeiter teilweise mit Leiterwagen vor den Werkstoren ab,
um die sackweise ausgezahlten Noten zu den nächstgelegenen Läden zu bringen und dort gegen knappe Waren einzutauschen,
source_name: Deutscher Bundestag, Wissenschaftliche Dienste, 'Hyperinflation in Deutschland 1923' (2023)
note: This is the best wording found. 'Twice a day' is NOT stated by any source I opened; 'payment in the lunch break' is the documented form. Note 'teilweise' (in some cases).

claim: 3. Wages paid daily; notes collected in bags and suitcases
fragments: in many places wages were being paid daily
People collected notes in bags and suitcases
crowded into shops to exchange their money for goods
Oft erfolgten die Lohnzahlungen täglich.
Geldtransport für Lohnauszahlung, 1923
source_name: Deutsche Bundesbank, 'Inflation - lessons learnt from history' (15 Oct 2012); Michael Kunzel, 'Die Inflation', LeMO, Deutsches Historisches Museum (14 Sep 2014)
note: First three fragments Bundesbank, last two LeMO (the last is a photo caption). Both say 'in many places' / 'often', not everywhere.

claim: 3. Payday scenes: lorry of notes, dash to the shops, relatives waiting to take the money
figures: A factory worker: payday every day at 11:00 a.m., a five-ton lorry of paper money in the forecourt, bundles thrown out, a dash to the nearest shop. Teachers paid at 10:00 a.m. brought the money to the playground, where relatives took the bundles and hurried off.
fragments: A factory worker described payday, which was every day at 11:00 a.m.:
At 11:00 in the morning a siren sounded, and everybody gathered in the factory forecourt,
where a five-ton lorry was drawn up loaded brimful with paper money.
They read out names and just threw out bundles of notes.
As soon as you had caught one you made a dash for the nearest shop
Teachers, paid at 10:00 a.m., brought their money to the playground,
where relatives took the bundles and hurried off with them.
source_name: George J.W. Goodman ('Adam Smith'), Paper Money (1981), pp. 57-62, excerpt on PBS Commanding Heights
note: A popular book by a financial journalist; the worker is not named and no source is given on the page. This is the nearest documented wording to 'wives waited at the factory gates': it says RELATIVES of TEACHERS at the PLAYGROUND. 'Wives at the factory gates' and 'workers were given time off to shop' were NOT FOUND in any source I opened.

claim: 3. How often wages were really paid (qualification)
figures: Kuczynski (1925): wages went from monthly to weekly, then twice a week 'and even oftener'. His Table 49 follows the paydays 'observed by most of the large establishments' 1 Oct-15 Nov 1923: a skilled Berlin chemical worker got 500 million marks on 1 Oct and 'had to live on those 500,000,000 marks four days'. Kroner, 26 Aug 1923: a note 'paid out today as a weekly wage'. Betty Scholem's family print shop, 15 Oct 1923: wages paid on Friday, 'the wage of this week' 8 billion.
fragments: With the depreciation of the money it became necessary to pay wages weekly.
When the depreciation oontinued, 1t became unavoidable to pay wages twice a week, and even oftener.
had to live on those 500,000,000 marks four days
The piece of paper, the spanking brandnew bank note, still moist from the printers, paid out today as a weekly wage
Der Lohn dieser Woche beträgt vorläufig 8 Milliarden,
source_name: R.R. Kuczynski, Postwar Labor Conditions in Germany, US Bureau of Labor Statistics Bulletin 380 (March 1925), pp. ~20 and 125-134; Kroner (1923); Betty Scholem (1923)
read_how: page text (Kuczynski is OCR; the misprints are in the scan)
note: Daily pay was real 'in many places' but not universal: three primary sources show weekly or twice-weekly pay in Berlin as late as August-November 1923. Say 'in many factories', not 'everyone'.

claim: 3. Laundry baskets, wheelbarrows, baskets, briefcases of money
fragments: Das Geld wird in Wäschekörben angekarrt
Geld wurde in Schubkarren transportiert, Bündel als Heizmaterial zweckentfremdet, die Rückseite als Schmierpapier benutzt.
Money was transported in wheelbarrows, bundles were misused as heating material,
bevor das Geld in Waschkörben davongetragen wurde.
big briefcases like this one were used as wallets.
grocery shopping with baskets full of money
source_name: Planet Wissen (WDR; photo caption and text); Prof. Hans Frambach, Univ. Wuppertal; Andreas Austilat, Tagesspiegel 17 Nov 2013; De Nederlandsche Bank (a briefcase with over 500 thousand-mark notes in its collection); David A. Price reviewing Frederick Taylor, The Downfall of Money, Richmond Fed Econ Focus 2014
note: Laundry baskets rest on a photo caption and a newspaper feature; wheelbarrows on a broadcaster's page and a professor's interview, none with a primary source. The firmly sourced containers are bags, suitcases, sacks and handcarts (Bundesbank, Bundestag). LeMO also mentions pastors holding out a laundry basket for the collection (reader's paraphrase, not verbatim).

claim: 4. Shops: prices changing during the day; opening hours tied to the exchange-rate announcement; closures
fragments: Ladenöffnungszeiten richteten sich nach den Bekanntgabeterminen für aktuelle Wechselkurse.
Parallel dazu stiegen die Preise nicht nur täglich, sondern stündlich.
Inflation skyrocketed, reaching its peak in November, when prices often rose several times in a single day
traders were constantly increasing their prices
others closed their businesses altogether
Shops restricted their hours and covered their windows with iron shades.
Viele Läden bunkerten ihre Bestände und Vorräte
This is no joke, this is reality, written seriously with a pencil, hung in the shop window and seriously read.
source_name: LeMO (Kunzel); Volker Ullrich, APuZ/bpb 20 Jan 2023; GHDI editors' abstract; Deutsche Bundesbank; Smithsonian Magazine; Planet Wissen; Kroner 1923
note: NOT FOUND in any source opened: the word 'multiplier' / 'Schlüsselzahl', a noon announcement of the dollar rate, or shops closing at midday to re-mark prices. The documented wording is the LeMO sentence (opening hours followed the times the exchange rates were announced). Bresciani-Turroni (p. 342, summer 1922) says traders 'adopted the practice of expressing prices in a foreign' currency. A Feb 1923 Berlin newspaper clipping describes shopkeepers pricing off last week's pound rate. A review of Taylor's book says stores 'sought retail clerks with banking experience'.

claim: 5. Restaurants and coffee: the price rose while the customer sat there
figures: Three different versions. (a) Victor Klemperer's diary, early August 1923, a station waiting room: board 6,000 M, waiter asked 12,000; when his wife objected the waiter took 6,000. (b) Goodman 1981: a Freiburg student, menu price 5,000, two cups, bill 14,000. (c) Britannica: 5,000 then 7,000 for the second cup. (d) De Nederlandsche Bank: 'according to some stories' 20,000 marks a cup in Berlin. LeMO: a restaurant bill could double during the meal.
fragments: Die Preistafel zeigte 6.000 M. Das verschwand, während sie trank.
Beim Kassieren verlangte der Kellner 12.000.
Dann zahlen Sie 6.000!
In Restaurants konnte sich die Zeche während der Mahlzeit verdoppeln.
A student at Freiburg University ordered a cup of coffee at a cafe.
The price on the menu was 5,000 Marks.
When the bill came, it was for 14,000 Marks.
ordering a cup of coffee for 5,000 marks and then a second whose cost had risen to 7,000 marks
According to some stories, you had to pay twenty thousand marks to get a cup of coffee in Berlin.
source_name: Volker Ullrich quoting Victor Klemperer's diary (APuZ/bpb 2023); LeMO; Goodman, Paper Money (1981) on PBS; Britannica; De Nederlandsche Bank
read_how: page text (the date 'early August 1923', the waiting room and that it was Eva Klemperer come from the reader's paraphrase of the same paragraph)
note: The '5,000 a cup, 8,000 by the time he finished' wording was NOT FOUND anywhere. The only version resting on a named primary source is Klemperer's (6,000 to 12,000, and the waiter backed down). The Freiburg-student story is unsourced on the PBS page and its figures differ from Britannica's. 'Waiters calling out new prices' NOT FOUND. The bpb page shows no footnote for the Klemperer entry, so the exact diary date is not confirmed.

claim: 6. Barter: goods instead of money
fragments: sell goods and services only in exchange for food and coal
Schließlich traten Naturalien (beispielsweise Lebensmittel, Zigaretten, Kohle) als Zahlungsmittel an die Stelle des Bargeldes.
Verkauf und Reparaturen im Tausch gegen Lebensmittel, 1923
Bezahlt wurden die Beerdigungen nicht mehr mit Geld, sondern mit Kohle zum Heizen.
People bought things they didn't need and used them to barter
a pair of shoes for a shirt, some crockery for coffee.
um dem Tausch von Ware gegen Ware begegnen zu können.
Wer etwas zum Tauschen hatte, tauschte.
source_name: Deutsche Bundesbank (2012); Reinhard Sturm, bpb (2011); LeMO photo caption (DHM, Inv. F 85/526); Armin Fuhrer, Berliner Zeitung 2022; Goodman 1981; Deutsche Bundesbank, Das Papiergeld im Deutschen Reich 1871-1948 (1965), p. 83; Tagesspiegel 2013
note: Documented in general terms: food, coal, cigarettes; a DHM photograph of a shop selling and repairing in exchange for food; funerals paid in coal (Berliner Zeitung, no source given). NOT FOUND in any source opened: cinemas or theatres taking eggs, butter or briquettes for tickets, or doctors asking for food. The Federal Trust essay ('three lumps of last winter's coal for a loaf of bread', 'two old candles for half a kilo of sausage') is an imagined first-person journey without sources: do not use as fact.

claim: 7. Notgeld: who issued it and how much
figures: LeMO: more than 5,800 towns, municipalities and firms issued their own notes; over 700 trillion (700 x 10^18) marks of Notgeld in all; more than 2,800 kinds of value-stable notes. Bundesbank 1965, from Dr Keller's eight-volume catalogue: 5,849 issuers in the 1923 inflation (towns, districts, municipalities, post, railway, many industrial firms); 562 issuers of value-stable Notgeld; the Reichsbahn alone 114 trillion paper marks; the Bundesbank holds over 60,000 Notgeld notes from this period. Earlier periods: 452 issuers (1914), 1,532, 3,683 (small-change notes 1916-22), 664 (1922). bpb: Notgeld worth 200 trillion (10^18) marks. Feldman's estimate (via a UCL thesis): about half of all paper marks in circulation were Notgeld.
fragments: Deshalb wurden von mehr als 5.800 Städten, Gemeinden und Firmen eigene Notgeldscheine herausgegeben.
Insgesamt sind über 700 Trillionen Mark (700.000.000.000.000.000.000 M) als Notgeld
Schließlich kursierten mehr als 2.800 verschiedene wertbeständige Geldscheinsorten in Deutschland.
5849 Ausgabestellen auf, unter denen neben Städten, Kreisen, Gemeinden, Post und Eisenbahn
Unseren Katalog dieser Ausgaben könnte man ebenso als Adreßbuch der deutschen Industrie von 1923 benutzen.
Gemeinden und Großbetriebe gaben zusätzlich „Notgeld“ in Höhe von 200 Trillionen Mark aus.
Gerald Feldman estimates that around half of all paper marks in circulation were Notgeld.
source_name: LeMO (Kunzel, DHM); Deutsche Bundesbank, Das Papiergeld im Deutschen Reich 1871-1948 (1965), pp. 85-89; Reinhard Sturm, bpb; 'Money for Inflation: The German Notgeld, 1914-1923' (PhD thesis, UCL, c. 2021), p. 16 n. 2 citing Feldman, The Great Disorder, p. 785
note: LeMO (700 Trillionen) and bpb (200 Trillionen) give different totals: report both or neither. German 'Trillion' = 10^18, 'Billion' = 10^12. The thesis says 'it is near impossible to find exact numbers for the scale of Notgeld issuance in 1923'.

claim: 7. Value-stable Notgeld (wertbeständiges Notgeld)
figures: LeMO: notes denominated in rye, wheat, wood, tar, coal, sugar, bacon, electricity and gas. Bundesbank 1965: approved value-stable Notgeld had to read 'Mark Gold' or 'Pfennig Gold', up to 4.20 marks (exceptionally 8.40); part of it was denominated in goods instead; approved circulation about 200 million gold marks; total Notgeld in circulation on 15 Nov 1923 about 988 million gold marks. Wirtschaftsdienst, 2 Nov 1923: it had to be covered by deposited Gold Loan and redeemable in Gold Loan; Gold Loan pieces of 1 and 2 dollars.
fragments: Diese Scheine lauteten auf Roggen, Weizen, Holz, Teer, Kohlen, Zucker, Speck, Strom und Gas.
Ein Teil davon lautete auch nicht, wie vorgeschrieben, auf Gold, sondern auf Sachwerte.
bis zur Höhe von 4,20 Mark, in Ausnahmefällen bis 8,40 Mark
teils aber auch auf Gold, Dollar oder Sachwerte,
Im Endstadium der Inflation bedurfte die Wirtschaft eines wertbeständigen Geldes,
source_name: LeMO (Kunzel); Deutsche Bundesbank (1965), pp. 43-44, 83, 88-89; 'Der Zahlungsverkehr in Deutschland', Wirtschaftsdienst no. 44, 2 Nov 1923, pp. 1005-1006
read_how: page text (the Wirtschaftsdienst article is a poor OCR; only short phrases were verbatim)
note: 4.20 gold marks = 1 dollar, which is why notes were worth 'one dollar' or fractions of it.

claim: 7. Notgeld made of unusual materials
figures: Named in sources opened: leather, silk, linen, cardboard, porcelain (and Böttger stoneware), wood, pressed coal, printed aluminium foil, 'metal foil', cloth, ceramic; cut-up playing cards 'in one case' (1914).
fragments: materials such as cutlery, porcelain, cardboard, leather, pressed coal, silk or linen
the newly founded aluminum rolling mills in Baden-Württemberg produced Notscheine from printed aluminum foil.
an assortment of materials such as ceramic, wood, cloth, metal foil, cardboard and leather were used.

claim: 8/11. Notes worth less than paper: a million-mark note used as a notepad

The sentence itself ('worth less than the paper') was NOT FOUND in any authoritative source opened. Many 1923 notes were printed on one side only (Bundesbank captions: 'Rückseite unbedruckt'), which is why the back could be written on.

claim: 9. The thief who stole the basket and left the money
figures: Reported by the Guardian in early 1923 as 'a current story in Berlin': a woman, a basket, the basket stolen and the money left.

There is a current story in Berlin of a woman who went shopping with a basket to carry her paper money.
She put it down for a minute, and on looking round found that the basket had been stolen
but the paper money left behind!

note: The contemporary newspaper itself calls it 'a current story', i.e. a tale going round Berlin, not a reported event, and it was already circulating in EARLY 1923, months before the worst of the inflation. No source opened documents a wheelbarrow or suitcase version or a named victim. Say: 'a story went round Berlin that...'. For real theft LeMO says (reader's paraphrase) that thieves no longer took only purses but searched victims for valuables and even pulled gold teeth; the verbatim opening is 'Kriminelle stahlen nun nicht mehr nur Geldbörsen'.

NOT FOUND in any source opened: a paper shortage as such, delivery by aeroplane, lorry or train (only the unsourced factory-lorry story in Goodman), bank staff counting by weight or by the bundle (Frambach says only 'People calculated in bundles instead of bills.'), or the sentence 'worth less than the paper it was printed on'.

claim: 12. Wages against prices: documented examples
figures: Kuczynski (1925): a skilled Berlin chemical worker earned 38.88 marks a week before the war; on 1 Oct 1923 he received 500,000,000 marks, worth 10.16 pre-war marks, and had to live on it four days; real wages 1-4 Oct were 45.7% of pre-war; the billion marks received on 13 Oct 'were worth only 9.2 per cent of his real wages in pre-war times'; workers paid a day later than neighbours 'received real wages perhaps 20 per cent less'. Berlin bricklayers' real wages in the first seven months of 1923: 13 to 32% of pre-war; printers 14 to 40%. LeMO: real wages fell to about 40% of the pre-war level. Bresciani-Turroni: miners 47.7% of the pre-war wage in January 1923; upper-grade officials 44.5% of pre-war salary in September 1923. Berliner Zeitung (Fuhrer): Jan 1913 to Jan 1923 food for a family of five rose 1,366-fold (3,183-fold by February), an unskilled Berlin worker's wage 643-fold, a skilled married state worker's 888-fold. Berliner Zeitung (Brettin): an unemployed person got 21 billion marks for 29 Oct-3 Nov 1923.

claim: 13. Rent control: rents fell to almost nothing; who gained and who lost
figures: Kuczynski (1925): legal rent was based on the rent of 1 July 1914; rent-restriction laws kept rents (in dollars) to one-tenth in 1921, one-fiftieth in 1922 'and to one one-hundredth or less in 1923'. Reichsmietengesetz 1922 tied increases to the 1914 'peace rent'; tenant protection law passed 1 June 1923, in force 1 October 1923; by August 1923 rents had been raised 'by 2,500 to 40,000 per cent' (Berliner Mieterverein). From 1 April 1924 owners paid a house-rent tax, in Prussia up to 48% of the peace rent.

claim: Commonly repeated claims that the sources opened contradict or qualify
figures: (1) Tram ride 50 billion on 2 Dec 1923 and 600 marks on 9 June 1923: the Statistisches Reichsamt table has 150 billion from 22 Nov and 400 marks until 10 June. (2) 'Wages were paid daily or twice a day': daily 'in many places' and in the lunch break, but weekly or every few days in several Berlin primary sources of Aug-Nov 1923; 'twice a day' not found. (3) The coffee story exists in at least four versions with different numbers; only Klemperer's is tied to a diary. (4) The thief and the basket: the Guardian called it 'a current story in Berlin' in early 1923. (5) Wallpaper: one agency photograph, of one-mark notes. (6) Notgeld of leather, silk, porcelain: mostly collector issues of 1917-1922, not money of autumn 1923. (7) 'Landlords were ruined': they lost rent income but kept debt-free buildings. (8) Bread at '201 / 233 / 399 / 428 billion': all from one official table, for different dates (Nov average, 19 Nov, Dec average, 26 Nov), per kilo of rye bread in Berlin; '260 billion' is per POUND on 1 Dec. (9) The famous '2 December 1923' price list is from after stabilisation (the mark was fixed on 20 Nov; the Rentenmark was issued from 15 Nov). (10) Total Notgeld: 700 Trillionen (LeMO) versus 200 Trillionen (bpb). (11) 'A wheelbarrow of money would not buy a newspaper': a figure of speech in Goodman and Britannica with no price behind it. (12) Dollar at the peak: Britannica says 'one U.S. dollar was equivalent to 1,000 billion (a trillion) marks' by November 1923; the German official sources say 4.2 trillion (4,200,000,000,000) on 20 November.
